extracted.intended_audience: young artists, landscape painters, art students, and art critics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for evaluating and producing landscape painting: truth of light/atmosphere, relation of background to figures, appropriate finish, color handling, style-as-means, and truthful study of nature (including mountains, foreground detail, and aerial space).

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness of light and atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Sky and atmospheric light must be rendered with absolute truth: clear blues gradated to the horizon, faithful rendering of cirri, rain clouds, and the wandering of light among hills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and counterexamples provided: Giovanni's sky described as 'absolute truth' with cautious gradation and glowing cirri; Claude first attempted 'realization of actual sunshine in misty air'; Titian rarely paints sunshine but an opalescent twilight; Turner and later masters carry out principles of aerial color. Anti-patterns: crude or conventionally flat skies; failure to gradate or to account for aerial subduing of color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background must have meaning and necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Every element in the background should be meaningful and necessary in reference to the figures; backgrounds should not be mere ornament or unrelated incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Titian's St. Jerome is praised as nearly faultless because 'there is nothing that is not of meaning and necessity in reference to the figures.' Anti-pattern: backgrounds added without relation to subject, merely decorative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotion must be conveyed through genuine feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects produced by strong emotion in painting must be seen through the medium of that emotion—cold-hearted observance or systematic imitation of emotional results is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin warns that works born of strong emotion are 'ill seen unless through the medium of such emotion' and that cold imitation will lead to false conclusions. Anti-pattern: mechanically reproducing highly emotive effects without the underlying feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate level of detail according to place and claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Detail and elaboration should be distributed according to where the eye is intended to rest: suggest in less important areas, elaborate where the picture claims attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Titian's St. Jerome: large features slightly executed where not meant for close inspection, but ivy and a lizard on a rock are drawn 'with the greatest accuracy' where the eye should dwell. Scoring note: overworking unimportant areas or under-detailing focal areas are faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style as the necessary means to express truth (not mannerism)
rubrics_metrics.description: An artist's manner or 'style' is justified only when it is the best or only means to express the particular truth the artist desires; persisted habits of execution without such necessity are base mannerism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Prout's reed-pen outline is not mere manner but necessary to express crumbling stone; conversely, conventional manner where the artist 'desires nothing and feels nothing' is condemned. Advice: distinguish virtuous, necessary manner from derivative convention; avoid affectation and showy tricks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conventional or careless treatment of local materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Architectural forms, mountains, sea, and sky should not be treated by rote repetition of conventional forms but studied in their particular truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tintoret's Venetian scenery criticized as 'conventional and careless' (sea distinguished from sky only by darker green); Leonardo's rock outlines called grotesque without feeling. Anti-pattern: repeating the same sky/mountain forms 'again and again for centuries.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Color modulation for distance (aerial perspective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distant (warm or intense) colors are subdued by the air and differ in quality from identical local colors in the foreground; distant blues and roses have a gray or warm undercurrent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fielding criticized for using 'crude color' in distances; Ruskin: 'the warm colors of distance... are subdued by the air' and 'the blue of distance... is not the blue of a bright blue flower.' Mastery of this modulation is 'perhaps the last attainment of the great landscape colorist.' Anti-pattern: using pure local color for distant planes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit light to shadow to express sunshine
rubrics_metrics.description: Colors and tones must be fitted so that light and shadow together express sunlight convincingly; local color alone without correct relation to shadow will look like overcharged color not sunshine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fielding is faulted for foregrounds that 'assume the aspect of overcharged local color instead of sunshine' because he disregards fitting light to shadow. Good examples: Giorgione, Titian, Tintoret, Turner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreground should be imaginatively necessary or botanically/geologically accurate
rubrics_metrics.description: A foreground must either be a deeply-studied, inventive whole (every part necessary to the other) or else realistically studied in botanical/geological detail so the eye can rest upon it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two acceptable virtues: Turner's studied imaginative foregrounds (Liber Studiorum) or faithful botanical realization of early masters. Criticism of Fielding: foregrounds are 'scattered and inessential' with no point for the eye to rest; lacking both invention and accurate study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve accidental effects where they serve the truth; avoid overworking
rubrics_metrics.description: Loose or accidental handling is acceptable when it is the only means to express a natural accidental quality; overworking that removes this accident is destructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: David Cox's loose execution is defended as the only means to express moisture and accidental parts of nature; Fielding's reworking removes the 'virtue, playfulness, and freedom of accident.' Rule: do not overfinish to the loss of natural spontaneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mere display of dexterity or technical bravado
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise of manual dexterity for its own sake, or painting to show off skill, is a vice; art should be directed by affection for the subject and truth of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Salvator accused of painting for dexterity with 'no love of any kind'; many Dutch landscapists display 'manual dexterities' while rejecting what is great in nature. Anti-pattern: producing work whose chief aim is technical display rather than expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bold licenses must be justified and atoned for
rubrics_metrics.description: Artistic liberties (oblique horizons, unusual shadow directions, rainbow next to sun, etc.) are permissible among masters whose grasp of nature is certain, but the greatness of the painter consists in atoning for such sacrifices of actuality by higher truth of feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rubens' bold liberties (oblique horizon, shadows at right angles) are accepted because of his certain grasp of nature; admonition to young artists: licenses require compensation ('atoning').

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific study required for faithful mountain painting
rubrics_metrics.description: Faithful representation of mountain scenery requires particular study and practice (often via watercolour); historically there are few genuine mountain drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin notes almost no faithful mountain painting among elder art except a faded Masaccio background; he cites Robson and David Cox as notable modern practitioners who express mountain stillness and color. Implication: specialized study of mountain forms and lichens necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rendering of space and aerial color (painting of Space)
rubrics_metrics.description: Large spaces of air and the slightness/confusion of touch that expresses luminous objects through space must be rendered to convey the sense of space; aerial color principles are essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tintoret praised as 'the painter of Space' for introducing slightness and confusion of touch expressive of luminous objects seen through air; these principles influenced Turner. Good practice: use touch and color to convey atmospheric depth rather than merely outlining forms.
